relevance_reason: The paper reports a family in which two brothers with fatal early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy carried compound heterozygous CACNA1A frameshift variants, and a third brother probably had the same genotype. This is biallelic CACNA1A disease, which is the subject of DEE42B.

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) reported 3 brothers born to non-consanguineous parents with a rapidly progressive, fatal, early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The leading features were severe muscular hypotonia from the newborn period (floppy infant), refractory early-onset seizures with deep apneic spells, and optic atrophy. The first child died at 5 months with suspected sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) after neonatal-onset hypotonia; he was not investigated.
quotes: The male infant born as the first child of seemingly healthy young, non-consanguineous parents died at the age of 5 months with suspicion of sudden infant death of infancy (SIDS). Neonatal-onset muscular hypotonia was noted

The leading clinical symptoms in the index case (II-4) and two of his siblings (II-1, II-2) were severe muscular hypotonia (floppy infant), plus refractory early-onset epileptic seizures and deep apneic spells, as well as optic atrophy.

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) described child II-2, who had hypotonia from the first week of life. At 5 months he was admitted with seizures, respiratory problems, dysphagia and severe hypotonia. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia, and PEHO syndrome was suspected; the table also lists blindness, edema, optic atrophy and cerebellar hypoplasia, while the text describes brain MRI as unrevealing. Multiple antiseizure drugs had no lasting effect, he needed tube feeding and transient ventilation, and he died at 14 months.
quotes: The boy was admitted at the age of 5 months for further diagnostics and treatment of epileptic seizures, respiratory problems as well as dysphagia and severe muscular hypotonia. EEG showed hypsarrhythmia during awake state as well as during sleep.
Based on clinical symptoms, PEHO (progressive encephalopathy, edema, hypsarrhythmia, optic atrophy) syndrome was suspected.
Blindness, severe muscular hypotonia, edema, optic atrophy, swallowing disorder (tube feeding) | DEE | PB, LEV, TPM, pyridoxine HCI, CZB, DEX, VGB | Cerebellar hypoplasia

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) described the index patient (II-4), who was hypotonic at birth and had his first seizures at 4 weeks. He went on to develop severe hypotonia with absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory and swallowing insufficiency, and many seizures a day: bilateral clonic and myoclonic seizures with gaze rigidity and apneic spells. EEG showed burst suppression at 4 weeks and, by 5 months, generalized background slowing with multifocal sharp waves. MRI was normal, treatment helped only transiently, and he died of respiratory insufficiency at age 2 years (2.5 years in the table).
quotes: the boy developed signs of an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy showing severe muscular hypotonia with absent deep tendon reflexes, respiratory and swallowing insufficiency, as well as highly frequent seizures.

The semiology of the multiple daily seizures was characterized by gaze rigidity, paleness, and bilateral clonic seizures and apneic spells, as well as myoclonic seizures. Electroencephalography revealed burst suppression (Figure 1A).
The patient died at the age of 2 years due to respiratory insufficiency.

findings.statement: In the index patient (II-4), Mammadova et al. (2024) found compound heterozygous frameshift variants in CACNA1A (NM_001127222.1) by trio exome sequencing: c.2602delG (p.Ala868Profs*24), inherited from the mother, and c.5476delC (p.His1826Thrfs*30), inherited from the father. Exome sequencing of material from his deceased brother II-2 found the same 2 variants; no material was available from brother II-1. Neither variant was in gnomAD or ClinVar, both were predicted to cause loss of function, and both were classified as pathogenic under ACMG criteria.
quotes: Exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygosity for two pathogenic CACNA1A (NM_001127222.1) variants in the index patient (II-4). Exome sequencing also confirmed these two variants in material from deceased child II-2.

None of the two variants was included in gnomAD or in ClinVar databases, at this point. Both variants are predicted to result in loss of function, either by truncation or nonsense mediated mRNA decay.

Trio-Exome sequencing identified an additional heterozygous pathogenic variant in the CACNA1A gene, c.5476delC, p.(His1826Thrfs*30) in the index patient and child 2, which was inherited from the asymptomatic father.

findings.statement: In the same family, Mammadova et al. (2024) found that the mother and a maternal uncle carried c.2602delG (p.Ala868Profs*24) in the heterozygous state and had episodic ataxia type 2. The mother had chronic headache, ataxic gait, dizziness, hand tremor and mild intellectual deficits, and she had seizures at 2 to 3 years of age. The father was heterozygous for c.5476delC and had no neurological symptoms.
quotes: Some years after birth of child II-3, episodic ataxia type 2 was diagnosed in the mother and one of her brothers due to a heterozygous frameshift pathogenic variant in the CACNA1A gene [c.2602delG, p.(Ala868Profs*24)].
The father had no specific neurological symptoms. He was heterozygous for a pathogenic variant in the CACNA1A gene [c.5476delC heterozygous, p.(His1826Thrfs*30)].

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) described a fourth brother (II-3), who carried a single heterozygous CACNA1A variant and had a milder phenotype. He was evaluated at age 5 years for episodic unsteady gait, dizziness and decreased vigilance, and he had mild intellectual impairment, learning disability, ADHD and primary generalized epilepsy that responded to levetiracetam; MRI was normal. The text says he carried the maternal c.2602delG variant, whereas Table 1 lists the paternal c.5476delC variant.
quotes: Child II-3 was found to be heterozygous for the maternal CACNA1A variant c.2602delG, p.(Ala868Profs*24).

The male child, born after an uneventful pregnancy, was referred at the age of 5 years for evaluation of an episodic, unsteady gait, dizziness and decreased vigilance. Clinical evaluation showed mild intellectual impairment and learning disability.
Child II-3 | 10 years, M | Heterozygous c.5476delC p.(His1826Thrfs*30)

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) compared their patients with 9 previously reported individuals from 4 families who had biallelic CACNA1A variants. They concluded that biallelic truncating loss-of-function variants were associated with severe, early-onset, fatal epileptic encephalopathy, which supported a correlation between how deleterious the biallelic variants were and how severe the phenotype was. They noted that heterozygous relatives were either asymptomatic or had milder phenotypes, and they considered CACNA1A-related disease to show both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance.
quotes: Our finding of bi-allelic truncating variants being associated with a severe, early onset epileptic encephalopathy with fatal outcome supports a genotype–phenotype correlation regarding deleteriousness of bi-allelic LOF variants and severity of the phenotype.
CACNA1 therefore belongs to the growing list of genes with co-dominantly or both autosomal dominantly and autosomal recessively inherited diseases.

findings.statement: Mammadova et al. (2024) proposed that ictal apneic spells were the most likely cause of death in the 2 brothers with proven variants. They also suggested that the brother diagnosed with SIDS probably died of ictal apnea.
quotes: In our patients, ictal apneic spells associated with subtle orofacial (child II-2) or epileptic spasms and generalized clonic seizures (child II-4) were the most prominent seizure type and most probably the cause of death in both brothers with the proven pathogenic variants.

relevance_reason: Case report of a child with compound heterozygous CACNA1A variants causing severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with progressive cerebellar atrophy (biallelic/recessive DEE42B), plus a summary of previously reported biallelic cases.

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reported a girl, born to nonconsanguineous White British parents, with a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. She had hypotonia and a weak suck from birth. At 5 months she had an alternating convergent squint and delayed visual maturation. At 6 months, after low-grade fever, she developed tonic-clonic status epilepticus. Her seizures did not respond to multiple antiepileptic drugs, and she needed repeated admissions for intractable seizures, chest infections, and respiratory arrests. She also needed gastrostomy because of poor bulbar function.
quotes: The index child (female) was born at term via a normal vaginal delivery following an uneventful pregnancy. Head circumference and weight at birth were 25th–50th centile. She had hypotonia and weak suck.

At 6 months, following the third routine scheduled immunizations, she developed low‐grade fever. Tonic–clonic status epilepticus ensued, resulting in admission to pediatric intensive care unit for ventilatory support and seizure management.

Over the next 3 years she required more than 20 admissions to hospital for chest infections, intractable seizures, and respiratory arrests requiring prolonged ventilatory support. She required a percutaneous gastrostomy due to poor bulbar function.

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reported that at 3 years the girl had secondary microcephaly, occasional myoclonus, and profound hypotonia, with no spasticity and no purposeful movement. By age 9 she had fixed flexion contractures and no distinctive dysmorphic features. At 9 to 10 years she still had generalized tonic-clonic seizures several times a week. At age 10, her Vineland composite score of 26 indicated severe intellectual disability, and she had impaired function across all social domains.
quotes: On physical examination at age 3 years, she had secondary microcephaly (head circumference <0.4th centile). Occasional myoclonus was observed. There were no signs of spasticity.
At age 9, she had fixed flexion contractures in her elbows, hips, and knees. There were no distinctive dysmorphic features (Figure 1).
Vineland Adaptive Scales, 3rd edition (Sparrow et al., 2016) composite score was 26, corresponding to severe ID.

phenotypes.text: flexion contractures of elbows, hips, knees

phenotypes.hpo_label: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with generalized onset

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reported that the girl's brain MRI at 6 months showed mild cerebellar hypoplasia and a thin corpus callosum. By 3 years, MRI showed cerebellar volume loss involving both hemispheres, the vermis, and the middle cerebellar peduncles, along with mild cerebral volume loss. By age 8, EEG was dominated by continuous focal sharp and slow wave complexes over the posterior regions, with brief tonic seizures. Nerve conduction studies, EMG, electroretinography, and audiology were normal.
quotes: MRI at 6 months (Figure 2a) showed no cerebral malformation and age‐appropriate myelination, but mild cerebellar hypoplasia and thin corpus callosum.
MRI at 3 years (Figure 2b) showed cerebellar volume loss involving both hemispheres, vermis and middle cerebellar peduncles.
By age 8 years, recordings were dominated by continuous focal sharp and slow wave complexes over the posterior regions, plus brief tonic seizures which were not localized or lateralized.

phenotypes.text: focal sharp and slow wave complexes on EEG
phenotypes.hpo_label: EEG with focal sharp slow waves

findings.statement: Using a next-generation sequencing panel for epileptic encephalopathy, Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) found that the girl was compound heterozygous for 2 CACNA1A variants, which they confirmed by Sanger sequencing. One was a maternally inherited 2-bp deletion, c.2042_2043delAG (NM_001127221.2), predicted to cause a frameshift and premature termination (p.Gln681ArgfsTer100). This truncating variant had previously been reported as pathogenic in episodic ataxia type 2, with variable expressivity, and the authors classified it as pathogenic by ACMG/AMP criteria. The mother, who carried this variant, had no neurological symptoms.
quotes: Two heterozygous sequence changes in CACNA1A were identified, and confirmed via Sanger sequencing.
NM_001127221.2 c.2042_2043delAG, p.(Gln681ArgfsTer100) was maternally inherited

The maternally inherited truncating variant has been previously reported as a pathogenic change associated with Episodic Ataxia 2, with variable expressivity within families (Denier et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2006; van den Maagdenberg et al., 2002).

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reported that the girl's second CACNA1A variant was a paternally inherited c.1693G>A transition (NM_001127221.2), resulting in a glu565-to-lys (E565K) substitution. The variant was absent from gnomAD and lay within an ion transport domain in a missense-constrained region. It affected a highly conserved residue and was predicted deleterious by SIFT and MutationTaster, but it remained a variant of uncertain significance by ACMG/AMP criteria. The father, who carried this variant, had infrequent mild migraines without hemiplegia and was suspected of having mild learning difficulties.
quotes: NM_001127221.2 c.1693G>A, p.(Glu565Lys) was paternally inherited
This variant has not been reported in The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD 2.2.1, https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/) and therefore is considered very rare.
The child's father suffered from infrequent non‐severe migraines, which were not associated with motor symptoms or hemiplegia. Mild learning difficulties were suspected but not formally documented.

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) noted that, unlike in previously reported biallelic families, the heterozygous carrier parents in this family showed no clear signs of a CACNA1A-associated syndrome. They suggested that the effect of calcium channel dysfunction is dose-dependent: monoallelic variants cause a highly variable spectrum, whereas biallelic variants cause severe, progressive neurologic disease. They also noted that this case shows the potential for a recessive diagnosis in an apparently sporadic disorder.
quotes: In contrast to previously reported biallelic cases, parents carrying these monoallelic variants did not display clear signs of a CACNA1A-associated syndrome.

Collectively, these cases suggest a dose‐dependent effect of calcium channel dysfunction: monoallelic variants are associated with a highly variable spectrum ranging from asymptomatic to motor‐only syndromes to epilepsies and cognitive impairment; biallelic variants lead to severe and progressive neurological symptoms and cognitive disabilities.
This case illustrates the potential for a recessive diagnosis in an apparently sporadic disorder in which a de novo cause is initially considered more likely.

findings.statement: Wong-Spracklen et al. (2022) reviewed this case together with earlier reports of biallelic CACNA1A variants. They identified consistent features as infantile hypotonia, treatment-refractory seizures beginning in the first 6 months of life, cerebral visual impairment, profound developmental delay with prominent and persistent motor impairment, and progressive cerebellar changes on MRI.
quotes: Consistent features which may aid variant interpretation and clinical management are infantile hypotonia, treatment‐refractory seizures with onset during first 6 months of life, cerebral visual impairment, profound developmental delay with prominent and persistent motor impairments, and progressive cerebellar changes on MRI.

relevance_reason: The paper reports the first patient with a homozygous loss-of-function CACNA1A variant, which is biallelic CACNA1A disease (DEE42B). Only the abstract was available, and it gives no variant or detailed clinical information.

findings.statement: Arteche-López et al. (2021) reported the first patients with homozygous disease-related variants in three genes previously associated with dominant inheritance. One of these was a homozygous loss-of-function variant in the CACNA1A gene. The patient had a more severe clinical phenotype than the typical dominant form, and the authors suggested that codominant or recessive inheritance could explain the difference.
quotes: We report the first patients harboring homozygous disease-related variants in three genes that were previously associated with dominant inheritance: a loss-of-function variant in the CACNA1A gene and two missense variants in the RET and SLC20A2 genes, respectively.
All patients presented with a more severe clinical phenotype than the corresponding typical dominant form.
We suggest that co-dominant or recessive inheritance for these three genes could explain the phenotypic differences from those documented in their cognate dominant phenotypes.

variants.as_reported: loss-of-function variant in the CACNA1A gene

relevance_reason: Reports sibs with compound heterozygous CACNA1A mutations causing early-onset epileptic encephalopathy with progressive atrophy — the defining biallelic DEE42B phenotype.

findings.statement: Reinson et al. (2016) described 2 sibs, a sister and brother, who were normal at birth but developed daily recurrent seizures in early infancy with concomitant extreme muscular hypotonia, hypokinesia, and global developmental delay. Brain MRI showed progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy. By 5 years of age, both were blind and bedridden with profound developmental delay; the elder sister died at that age.
quotes: Both patients were normal at birth, but developed daily recurrent seizures in early infancy with concomitant extreme muscular hypotonia, hypokinesia, and global developmental delay.
The brain MRI images showed progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy.
At the age of 5, both patients were blind and bedridden with a profound developmental delay. The elder sister died at that age.

findings.statement: In 2 sibs with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy and progressive cerebral, cerebellar, and optic nerve atrophy, Reinson et al. (2016) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the CACNA1A gene by exome sequencing: a missense mutation c.4315T>A (p.Trp1439Arg) in exon 27 and a 7-bp deletion c.472_478delGCCTTCC (p.Ala158Thrfs*6) in exon 3. Their parents and 2 sibs were each heterozygous for one of the mutations.
quotes: Exome sequencing detected biallelic mutations in CACNA1A: A missense mutation c.4315T>A (p.Trp1439Arg) in exon 27, and a seven base pair deletion c.472_478delGCCTTCC (p.Ala158Thrfs*6) in exon 3.
Their parents and two siblings were heterozygotes for one of those pathogenic mutations and expressed a milder phenotype.

findings.statement: Reinson et al. (2016) noted that the heterozygous carrier parents and 2 sibs of the affected children expressed a milder phenotype: both of them [as stated] had intellectual disability, and the mother additionally had adult-onset cerebellar ataxia with slowly progressive cerebellar atrophy.
quotes: Their parents and two siblings were heterozygotes for one of those pathogenic mutations and expressed a milder phenotype.
Both of them have intellectual disability and in addition the mother has adult onset cerebellar ataxia with a slowly progressive cerebellar atrophy.
